title: PostgreSQL: when to use it
description: The default-choice mindset: what PostgreSQL does well, where it struggles, and how to justify the choice (or an alternative) out loud.
source: Study notes: when and how to use PostgreSQL in system design interviews

questions.prompt: In a system design interview with no unusual requirements, how should you treat PostgreSQL?

options.text: As the default choice, then explain any reason you would deviate from it.
options.why: Right: starting from a strong general-purpose default is easier to defend.

options.text: As a last resort, only after proving every NoSQL option fails first.
options.why: It is the reverse: PostgreSQL is a safe starting point, not a last resort.

options.text: As a tool reserved for banks and other finance-only systems.
options.why: It suits many domains: e-commerce, content, analytics at reasonable scale.

options.text: As a poor choice for anything that needs to scale beyond one node.
options.why: Replication, partitioning and sharding take it much further than one node.

questions.explanation: Start with PostgreSQL and justify deviations. That is much stronger than starting with a niche store and arguing it beats PostgreSQL.

questions.prompt: Select all the needs where PostgreSQL is a particularly good fit.

options.text: Complex relationships between entities that need joins and foreign keys.
options.why: Yes: relational integrity is a core strength.

options.text: A mix of structured data and flexible semi-structured metadata (JSONB).
options.why: Yes: JSONB gives document-style flexibility in the same database.

options.text: Built-in full-text search and geospatial queries (with PostGIS).
options.why: Yes: these remove the need for extra systems in many designs.

options.text: Millions of writes per second with no joins and no transactions.
options.why: That is an extreme write-throughput case where other stores fit better.

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL combines relational integrity, flexible JSONB, search and geo features. Extreme write rates are where you start looking elsewhere.

questions.prompt: A telemetry pipeline must absorb millions of small writes per second with no joins. Which concern most weakens PostgreSQL here?

options.text: Every write needs a WAL entry and index updates, creating I/O bottlenecks.
options.why: Right: per-write durability and index maintenance cap throughput per node.

options.text: PostgreSQL cannot store timestamps accurately enough for telemetry.
options.why: It stores timestamps with microsecond resolution; precision is not the issue.

options.text: PostgreSQL has no way to run more than one server at a time.
options.why: It supports replication and sharding; the issue is write cost, not server count.

options.text: PostgreSQL rejects tables that contain more than a million rows.
options.why: There is no such limit; tables can hold far more than that.

questions.explanation: Per-write WAL and index costs, plus coordination across shards, make millions of writes per second a poor fit. Consider Cassandra or a queue plus batching.

questions.prompt: Users on three continents must all write locally with low latency, and the writes must stay globally consistent. What is the core PostgreSQL limitation?

options.text: Its single-primary design makes true active-active writes across regions hard.
options.why: Right: one region owns writes; multi-primary needs conflict handling PostgreSQL lacks.

options.text: It cannot create replicas outside the region where the primary runs in a typical production setup.
options.why: Cross-region replicas are possible; they are read-only copies.

options.text: It has no transactions that span more than one table at a time for most everyday workloads.
options.why: Multi-table transactions are a standard feature.

options.text: It stores data in a format that cannot be sent over a network.
options.why: Replication ships WAL over the network routinely.

questions.explanation: One primary accepts writes. Active-active needs something built for it: CockroachDB for global ACID, Cassandra or DynamoDB global tables for eventual consistency.

questions.prompt: Your access pattern is purely get/put by key, with no joins or ad hoc queries. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: PostgreSQL works but is overkill; Redis or DynamoDB fit the pattern better.
options.why: Right: MVCC, WAL and the planner add overhead you would not use.

options.text: PostgreSQL is the only database that can serve a key lookup quickly.
options.why: Many stores serve key lookups quickly; most do it with less overhead.

options.text: Key-value access patterns are impossible to model in a SQL table.
options.why: A two-column table models it fine; it is just not the best tool.

options.text: PostgreSQL requires a separate cache before it can answer any lookup under normal operating conditions.
options.why: It answers indexed lookups directly; a cache is an optimisation.

questions.explanation: Do not pay for a query planner and MVCC when you only need get/put. Pick the simpler store and say why.

questions.prompt: True or false: "NoSQL scales better, so we should not use PostgreSQL" is a strong justification on its own.

options.text: True
options.why: It is too broad to defend without a concrete requirement.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: you need a specific limit such as write rate or multi-region writes.

questions.explanation: Scalability alone is not a good reason to leave PostgreSQL; it handles large scale with replication, partitioning and sharding. Name the concrete requirement instead.

questions.prompt: A product needs relational data, flexible post metadata and basic text search. What is the simplest sound architecture?

options.text: PostgreSQL alone, using JSONB for metadata and full-text search for text.
options.why: Right: one system covers all three, with less to operate.

options.text: PostgreSQL for users, MongoDB for metadata and Elasticsearch for search as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: Three systems add operational and consistency cost the needs do not justify yet.

options.text: MongoDB alone, because it handles flexible metadata natively.
options.why: It loses relational integrity that the data model relies on.

options.text: Elasticsearch alone, because it can also store all the user records.
options.why: It is a search engine, not a transactional source of truth.

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL features often remove the need for MongoDB or Elasticsearch. Add them only when a requirement outgrows the built-ins.

questions.prompt: What does an interviewer usually want to see when you bring up PostgreSQL?

options.text: Informed architectural decisions about fit, trade-offs and scale.
options.why: Right: the interview tests design judgement, not administration.

options.text: A detailed walkthrough of MVCC and WAL internals from memory in the majority of deployments.
options.why: Too deep is a common trap unless the interviewer asks.

options.text: The exact syntax of every PostgreSQL configuration parameter.
options.why: Configuration trivia is not what a design interview measures.

options.text: A claim that PostgreSQL is better than every other database.
options.why: Overbroad claims without trade-offs sound weak.

questions.explanation: Be a decision-maker, not a DBA: relationships, consistency, query patterns and scale, with internals only when they change the decision.
